reason: The court adopted the derivative-title requirement under Partition Law section 52A, but the extracted statute cites Prevention of Frauds section 2 instead.
The court did hold that a prescription claimant must identify the corpus, but the cited Evidence Ordinance section is not the provision construed for that rule.
The quoted passage is the court's own reasoning for upholding restoration under the Civil Procedure Code's inherent-power jurisdiction.
The non-retrospectivity point was accepted by the court, but the supporting quote is expressly counsel's submission.
The holding is quoted, but the statement omits the court's material case-specific and equitable limitation on the relief ultimately granted.
The court treated consideration of the full devolution-of-title evidence in the partition action as the basis for refusing appellate interference.
The statement reflects the holding on rei vindicatio versus licensee or lessee ejectment, but the selected quote is only a vague transition sentence.
The impossibility principle was applied, but the quote is borrowed from legal literature and the cited Jaffna matrimonial-property section is not the provision for this rule.
The quoted statutory text directly supports the court's holding that the partition settlement failed for non-compliance with Civil Procedure Code section 408.
The court held that the tenant's unauthorised construction without the owner's permission defeated protected possession and justified eviction.
The arbitral-award rule is broadly correct, but the quote is from another case and the cited Civil Procedure Code section is not the Arbitration Act provision construed.
The court held that section 161 does not protect grant land from prescription between these parties, so the statement's conclusion is the opposite of the decision.
The court accepted that a mere traditional-measure discrepancy is not by itself enough to make a partition corpus unidentified.
The court applied accession as part of its holding that the defendant could not claim the house separately from the plaintiff's land.
The land-identification rule is central to the rei vindicatio dismissal, but Civil Procedure Code section 323 was only context for execution and was not the construed provision.
The court held that parol evidence may be led to prove a constructive trust under section 83 despite Prevention of Frauds and Evidence Ordinance objections.
The court answered the temple-property question affirmatively under the Buddhist Temporalities Ordinance, but the selected quote is from another judgment.
The court found on the facts that this plaintiff was not claiming a larger land, so the extracted statement turns a factual negative into an unsupported general rule with a wrong statute.
The court did require title and prior corpus identification for declaratory relief, but Civil Procedure Code section 432(2) was not the provision construed for that rule.
The result on ratification and third-party rights is broadly reflected, but the quote only covers ratification and the cited Prescription Ordinance section concerns a separate limitation point.
The court's own reasoning directly supports the holding that appeals from preliminary rulings would undermine the special bank-recovery procedure.
The selected passage is counsel's submission and the court's actual holding was narrower, namely that the affidavit was not invalid merely for lacking a further truth averment.

The court accepted the vendor-title obstacle to timely payment, but the statement omits the vendor fault and specific-performance context and wrongly cites Prevention of Frauds section 2 for this rule.
The quote supports the court's holding that interim relief should not lightly restrain parate execution absent a sustainable prima facie challenge.
The court held under Prevention of Frauds section 2 that signatures on a partition plan alone do not transfer or renounce co-ownership rights.
